sections.title: The Key Difference
sections.content: Misinformation is false information shared without intent to harm. Disinformation is false information deliberately created and spread to deceive. The difference is intent — and intent matters for how we respond.
bullets: Misinformation: Someone shares a false headline because they believe it is true
Disinformation: A state actor creates a fake news site to influence an election
Malinformation: True information shared with intent to harm (doxing, leaks)

sections.title: Why the Distinction Matters
sections.content: Misinformation requires education and fact-checking. Disinformation requires regulation, platform accountability, and legal consequences. Treating them the same leads to ineffective solutions.
bullets: Misinformation is fixed by teaching SIFT and media literacy
Disinformation requires platform policies and sometimes legal action
Knowing the difference helps you diagnose and respond correctly

sections.instruction: A bot network creates fake social media accounts to spread false voting information. This is:
sections.feedback: Disinformation — deliberately created and spread to deceive.

sections.explain: Disinformation is intentional deception. Misinformation is unintentional.

sections.statement: Sharing a false news article because you thought it was true is an example of disinformation.
sections.feedback: Without intent to deceive, it is misinformation, not disinformation.

sections.instruction: Match each scenario to the correct category.

pairs.right: Creating a fake news site to influence voters
Publishing someone's private address to harass them

sections.feedback: Intent and harm determine the category.

questions.argument: 'All false information online should be treated as disinformation.' Identify the issue:
options: It ignores the difference between intentional and unintentional falsehoods
questions.feedback: Misinformation (unintentional) and disinformation (intentional) require different responses.
